title: One day at a time
hookLine: Jesus: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof (Matthew 6:34)

lines: A LINE THAT SOUNDS LIKE A COURTHOUSE.
TODAY HAS ENOUGH OF ITS OWN.
cards: "Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." It sounds like something carved over an old courthouse door.
It's actually the last line of a short talk about worry in the Gospel of Matthew, and in the story Jesus says it to a crowd on a hillside.
The text calls them the multitudes: people with bills, harvests and children of their own to worry about. He doesn't tell them their troubles are imaginary. He tells them something stranger.
Today has enough of its own.

teach.h: TAKE NO THOUGHT: A TALK ABOUT WORRY.
teach.b: First, the instruction. In the King James Bible the passage keeps saying "take no thought." Readers sometimes hear that as don't plan.
The talk is about worry, the kind that runs ahead and chews on things that haven't happened.
Second, the birds and the flowers. "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them."

And then: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." In between, a question with a smile in it: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?"
Worry, it turns out, doesn't make anyone taller. Third, the closing line in full.

"Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Evil here means trouble, hardship. Notice what the line admits.
Today has trouble. It doesn't promise an easy day. It says one day's share is enough to carry, and tomorrow's share can wait for tomorrow.
The same sermon, a little earlier, holds the prayer Christians call the Lord's Prayer, with its line "Give us this day our daily bread." Bread for this day. Not a year's supply.
Some readers hear the two together: trust practiced one day at a time.
And the same shape turns up outside the church too, in recovery rooms and hospital waiting rooms: handle today. Just today.

how: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer each morning, asking for 'this day our daily bread', and turn to Matthew 6 in anxious seasons; recovery groups use the phrase 'one day at a time' in a similar spirit.

the teacher who said each day has trouble enough of its own

p: a talk about worry, not planning
they sow not, yet they are fed

s: Matthew 6:34 promises that today will have no trouble
it admits the day has trouble: 'sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.'
the line about daily bread comes from the same sermon in Matthew

games.q: it's 2am and a worry about next month shows up. what does Matthew 6:34 point toward?
o: solve next month now, while you're awake.
let tomorrow take thought for itself; today's share is enough.
games.why: "the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." it doesn't deny the trouble; it gives each day its own share.

practice: Bring up whatever is weighing on you and sort it gently: what belongs to today, a call, a meal, one conversation, and what belongs to a later day, the test next month, the bill next season.
Picture the later things on a shelf where they'll wait for their own day, and hold only today's share as you breathe. If you pray, you can ask for today's bread and nothing more.

wordCard.voice: Jesus, who told a hillside crowd that today has trouble enough of its own, and tomorrow's share can wait for tomorrow. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: 'sufficient, enough', the first word of 'sufficient unto the day' in Matthew 6:34 (the verse itself opens differently).

carryVoice: Your line: today is enough. One day's share is plenty to carry. Day seven hundred forty-eight, done.
